attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter. He presents the data wall as fact, not as someone else's view.

semantics.note: Unhedged claim that a wall is coming which generative AI can't get past, tied to running out of training data. The proposition keeps the data-exhaustion clause and gives no deadline, matching the source.

contract.note: Requiring proof of data exhaustion before judging the wall is a fair reading of 'as it runs out of training data'. 'Quickly-approaching' gives no date, and the contract rightly does not invent one.

evidence.note: Epoch's 2024 projection says public text would be used up between 2026 and 2032. It is a forecast, not proof that exhaustion happened.
DeepSeek-R1 shows reasoning gains from reinforcement learning, a possible workaround. It does not show that training data had run out.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows usable training data has run out, so neither a lasting ceiling nor a way past one can be judged. Both items are context only, and the evidence available by the cutoff does not settle the outcome.

attribution.note: Zitron's own unhedged assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'Will never, ever create' AGI is a firm forecast with no end date. 'Know nothing' is kept as stated. The contract treats it as an ambiguity and does not score it separately.

contract.note: The contract defines AGI as broad, independently accepted human-level generality, an ordinary reading. A 'never' claim can only be supported by an impossibility result, which is fair. The result depends on how AGI is defined, and the speaker gave no definition.

evidence.note: AGI Society (Sept 2026) says no test for AGI is generally accepted and does not accept the Astra evidence as AGI. That is not proof of impossibility.
ARC Prize (Sept 2026) reports strong GPT-6 Astra results on unfamiliar tasks but says saturating the benchmark is not proof of AGI.

reviews.rationale: This is an open-ended 'never' forecast. The packet shows major capability gains but no broadly accepted, independently verified transformer AGI, and no impossibility result. Neither the contradiction nor the support condition is met by the cutoff.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'Eventually, it will come for your livelihood' is an unhedged forecast with no deadline. The proposition rightly drops the personification ('wants us to stop thinking'), which is rhetoric.

contract.note: The plain reading, a threat to some people's paid work rather than to everyone's job, is an ordinary reading of the generic 'your'. A stricter reading requiring broad displacement could change the result.

evidence.note: September 2025 report: Salesforce support staff fell from about 9,000 to 5,000 as its AI agents took over work, and the roles are not being refilled. The facts rest on company disclosures, which the contract accepts as employer records.
Danish study of 2023–24 found no effect on earnings or hours in the occupations studied. Different setting and period. It limits broad claims but does not rule out a threat to particular roles.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met by a dated post-publication case: Salesforce stopped refilling thousands of support roles after AI took over their work. That event rests on company statements. The Danish study shows no broad earnings losses, so only the narrow 'threat to paid roles' reading holds.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: This captures the first clause, a softened observation ('does not appear'). The later clause about markets punishing investors is a separate conditional forecast and is not covered here.

contract.note: Reading 'returns' as net of costs and using Q1 2024 as the period are reasonable but are the evaluator's choices. The speaker gave no metric, comparison years, or group of businesses, so the interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: McKinsey survey (fielded Feb–Mar 2024) has self-reported gen-AI benefits mostly from 2023. It is not net of costs and has no comparison with the earlier booms.
Sequoia's June 2024 investor analysis argues AI infrastructure has weaker pricing power than CPU cloud. It is opinion, not measured returns.
Apple's 2014 figure is cumulative gross developer earnings. It shows no costs and no spread of profits, so it is only historical context.

reviews.rationale: No item gives a matched, cost-inclusive comparison of business returns from gen AI in Q1 2024 against the cloud and app-store booms. All items are context, so the evidence available by the cutoff does not settle the observation.
